text: This is a scenario built to illustrate a real and common tension, not an account of an actual company. Ridgeline Outfitters' checkout SLO allows a 43-minute error budget a month, and order-service runs on a node pool sized with roughly 35% headroom above average load, specifically to absorb the daily traffic peak without autoscaling lag causing timeouts.

Three weeks before the incident, a routine right-sizing pass -- the kind Chapter six teaches directly -- flags that node pool as over-provisioned at 52% average utilization, and recommends dropping from six nodes to four. The pull request merges cleanly, approved by two platform engineers who aren't on the SRE rotation for order-service, and the SLO's headroom assumption is never mentioned.

A flash-sale spike at 11:40 on a Tuesday is nothing unusual -- the six-node pool had absorbed it every time before. At four nodes, the autoscaler has to provision two more, and that four-minute bootstrap window is where checkout p99 latency crosses 800ms and the SLO breaches, burning 19 of the month's 43-minute error budget in one event.

The on-call engineer's first read looks like a routine autoscaling-lag problem, because nothing in the paging alert says a node pool was downsized three weeks earlier. The blameless postmortem from Lesson 28 pulls Lesson 29's trace data and Lesson 30's cost dashboard side by side -- the traces show pod scheduling delay dominating, a capacity problem, not a code defect.

Checking the node pool's own change history against that timestamp surfaces the three-week-old node_count change immediately, because the cost dashboard had already logged exactly when the spend drop took effect. The root cause isn't the autoscaler -- it's a legitimate cost optimization that removed headroom the SLO was quietly relying on, approved without anyone who understood that dependency.

The fix is a process gate, not a technology fix: any capacity change on an SLO-bound service now requires an SRE reviewer, and the right-sizing checklist states the current error budget and autoscaler warm-up time next to the proposed change. Lesson 32 closes the chapter by tracing this and every other capstone decision back through all eight chapters of the course.
